rules.quote: Use numerals with the percentage sign
rules.violation_condition: A numerical percentage is written without numerals and the percentage sign, outside the exceptions for sentence beginnings and imprecise everyday expressions.
when: Applies to numerical percentages in text.
At the start of a sentence, the percentage can be written out in words instead.
Everyday words can replace a percentage when a precise amount is not needed.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the repeated wording; G-2 and G-3 retain the exceptions without making them separate rules.

examples.note: The percentage sign immediately follows the number.
A space separates the number and percentage sign.

rules.quote: Don’t use a space between the number and the percentage sign.
rules.violation_condition: A space separates a number from its percentage sign.
rules.why: This is a distinct spacing check; E-2 assigns the adjacent Correct and Incorrect examples to it.

examples.note: The percentage uses decimal notation.

parts.quote: The price of Tapis oil is up by 0.25%.

examples.note: The percentage uses a fraction.

parts.quote: The price of Tapis oil is up by 1/4%.

rules.quote: Use decimals rather than fractions with the percentage sign.
rules.violation_condition: A fractional percentage is written using a fraction rather than decimal notation.
when: Applies when a percentage includes a fractional amount.
rules.why: This is a separate notation preference, and E-2 assigns the nearest examples to this body instruction rather than the preceding label.

covers.quote: Reword the sentence if possible, or write the percentage out in words.
You can use everyday words if a precise amount is not needed.

examples.note: The sentence-initial percentage is written in words.

parts.quote: Fifty-five per cent of the council’s revenue came from rates.

examples.note: The percentage does not begin the sentence.

parts.quote: Rates accounted for 55% of revenue.

examples.note: The numerical percentage begins the sentence.

parts.quote: 55% of the council’s revenue came from rates.

rules.quote: As for any number, avoid starting a sentence with the percentage.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with a percentage expressed in numerals.
when: A percentage written out in words can begin a sentence.
Rewording the sentence so the numerical percentage appears later also satisfies the rule.
Everyday words can be used when a precise amount is not needed.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the alternative ways of avoiding a sentence-initial numerical percentage within one check; G-3 treats the permission as an exception.

covers.quote: ‘Per cent’ and ‘percentage’ aren’t the same. The term ‘per cent’ is an adverb. The noun form is ‘percentage’.

examples.note: ‘Percentage’ supplies the noun.

parts.quote: Statistics show the percentage of Australians with university degrees is increasing.

examples.note: ‘Per cent’ is incorrectly used as a noun.

parts.quote: Statistics show the per cent of Australians with university degrees is increasing.

rules.quote: Use the correct form of the noun (percentage)
rules.violation_condition: ‘Per cent’ is used as a noun where ‘percentage’ is required.
when: Applies when the expression functions as a noun, rather than accompanying a numerical amount.
rules.why: G-4 keeps the heading and its grammatical explanation as one noun-choice rule.

covers.quote: ‘Percent’ is not Australian spelling.

rules.quote: ‘Per cent’ is written as 2 words in Australia.
rules.violation_condition: The expression ‘per cent’ is spelled as the single word ‘percent’.
when: Applies when the expression is written in words.
rules.why: G-4 combines the positive spelling convention and the rejection of its one-word alternative into one check.

covers.quote: Avoid using percentages to describe changes.
Tell people what the actual increase or decrease is.

examples.note: The change is given as an actual amount.

parts.quote: The application fee is now $70. This is a $20 increase from 1 January 2020.

examples.note: The increase is described using a percentage.

parts.quote: The application fee increased by 40% from $50 to $70 on 1 January 2020.

rules.quote: Don’t use percentages to describe change
rules.violation_condition: An increase or decrease is described using a percentage.
when: Applies to descriptions of increases or decreases, rather than proportions.
State the actual increase or decrease instead.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the heading, its direct restatement and the replacement wording into one change-description check.

covers.quote: Be concise when writing about percentages
Be concise when you write about percentages.

examples.note: The figures are presented in parentheses.

parts.quote: In 2019, population size increased in New South Wales (32%), Queensland (20%) and Victoria (19%).

examples.note: The figures remain in repetitive running prose.

parts.quote: In 2019, the largest sources of population growth were New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. New South Wales accounted for 32% of the population growth, Queensland 20%, and Victoria 19%.

rules.quote: When you use many percentages in body text, put the figures in brackets (parentheses) or use a list to simplify the text.
rules.specification: The page does not define ‘many’ or the span over which percentages should be counted. An agreed trigger is needed; no numerical threshold is inferred from the example.
rules.violation_condition: Body text contains many percentages in running prose without putting the figures in parentheses or presenting them in a list.
when: Applies to body text containing many percentages.
Parentheses and a list are alternative acceptable presentations.
rules.why: G-4 selects the actionable body instruction over its broad heading; G-2 keeps the two acceptable presentations together, and E-4 prevents inventing a threshold for ‘many’.
